items.value: Statement 2 only — the Lok Sabha first recognised a Leader of the Opposition in 1969
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is impossible on its own dates: the first Lok Sabha sat from 1952 to 1957, whereas the Swatantra Party was founded by C. Rajagopalachari only in 1959; the largest opposition party in that House was the Communist Party of India. Statement 2 is correct — Ram Subhag Singh of the Congress (O) was the first leader formally recognised as Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, in 1969. Statement 3 gets the threshold wrong: the Speaker's Direction requires a party to hold at least one-tenth of the total strength of the House, i.e. 55 members in a 543-member Lok Sabha, not 75.

items.value: All three — hard waxy leaves, tiny leaves and thorns instead of leaves are all xerophytic water-saving modifications
items.reasoning: Every one of the three is a textbook xerophytic adaptation. A thick, hard, waxy cuticle seals the leaf surface and cuts cuticular transpiration; reducing the leaf to a tiny blade cuts the surface area available for transpiration; and reducing leaves to thorns, as in cacti, removes the transpiring surface almost entirely while the stem takes over photosynthesis. Since none of the three can be excluded, the answer must be the all-inclusive option.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — Rajasthan tops the share of agricultural households, and Kerala's agricultural households draw most income from non-farm sources; the OBC figure is wrong
items.reasoning: In the NSSO 70th Round Situation Assessment Survey, Rajasthan recorded the highest proportion of agricultural households among its rural households (about 78 per cent), so statement 1 stands. Kerala was the standout state where a clear majority of agricultural households reported their largest income from sources other than agriculture, matching statement 3. Statement 2 is the error: OBCs accounted for roughly 45 per cent of the country's agricultural households, not a little over 60 per cent, so 'a little over 60 percent' overstates it by a wide margin.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the functional contrast is right, but the CPCB was created by statute, not by executive order
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is half right and therefore wrong: the NGT was indeed set up by the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, but the Central Pollution Control Board was constituted under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 — a statute, not an executive order. Statement 2 describes both bodies accurately: the NGT Act's own object is the effective disposal of environmental cases and relief of the higher courts' docket, while the CPCB's statutory functions under the Water Act and the Air Act are to promote the cleanliness of streams and wells and to improve air quality.

items.value: Statement 1 only — Parliament can add a law to the Ninth Schedule, but such laws are not immune from judicial review
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: laws are placed in the Ninth Schedule by a constitutional amendment passed by Parliament under Article 368, as has been done more than 280 times since the First Amendment of 1951. Statement 2 overstates the protection of Article 31B. In I. R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) a nine-judge bench held that any law inserted into the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 is open to challenge if it damages the basic structure, so courts can and do examine such laws.

items.value: The fee a bank charges a merchant for accepting customer payments made through the bank's debit cards
items.reasoning: The Merchant Discount Rate is the percentage of a card transaction's value that the acquiring bank deducts from the merchant for processing the payment; it is shared between the acquiring bank, the issuing bank and the card network. It is a cost borne by the merchant, which is why the RBI caps it to keep small merchants from refusing cards. Options A and D describe incentives paid to merchants and B describes cashback to customers — all money flowing towards the merchant or the customer, the opposite direction from the MDR.

items.value: Neither — NSG membership neither guarantees the latest nuclear technology nor confers NPT membership
items.reasoning: The Nuclear Suppliers Group is an export-control cartel whose members agree to common guidelines on what nuclear material, equipment and technology they will export; it is not a technology-sharing club, and actual transfers still depend on bilateral agreements, so membership does not by itself deliver 'the latest and most efficient nuclear technologies'. India's 2008 NSG waiver already opened nuclear commerce to it without membership, which shows the two are separable. Statement 2 is plainly wrong: NSG and NPT are separate instruments with separate accessions, and France participated in the NSG for years before it joined the NPT in 1992. The judgement call is on statement 1; if that were read generously the answer would be A.

items.value: Neither — the equalisation levy sits outside the Income Tax Act, and for that very reason no DTAA credit is available
items.reasoning: The six per cent equalisation levy on online advertisement payments to non-resident entities was enacted by Chapter VIII of the Finance Act, 2016 as a standalone levy, deliberately kept outside the Income Tax Act, 1961. That design choice is exactly what defeats statement 2 as well: because the levy is not an income tax, it falls outside the scope of the Double Taxation Avoidance Agreements, and non-resident entities cannot claim a foreign tax credit for it in their home jurisdiction.

items.value: Statements 1 and 3 only — the 60:40:20 debt target and Article 293(3) consent are right; the Centre's and States' liability figures are swapped
items.reasoning: Statement 1 reproduces the N. K. Singh FRBM Review Committee's headline recommendation: a general government debt ceiling of 60 per cent of GDP by 2023, split 40 per cent Centre and 20 per cent States. Statement 3 restates Article 293(3), under which a State cannot raise a loan without the Union's consent so long as any part of a loan made to it by the Union remains outstanding. Statement 2 reverses the figures — it is the Centre that carries liabilities of roughly half of GDP while the States carry around a fifth, not the other way round.

items.value: Statement 1 only — imports of edible oil do exceed domestic production, but customs duty is very much levied on them
items.reasoning: India meets well over half its edible oil demand through imports: annual imports have run at roughly 14-15 million tonnes against domestic edible oil production of about 7-8 million tonnes, so statement 1 holds for the period in question. Statement 2 is false on its face — customs duty is levied on imported edible oils and the rates on crude and refined palm, soyabean and sunflower oil were in fact raised sharply in 2017-18 to protect domestic oilseed growers.

items.value: Lala Lajpat Rai
items.reasoning: Lala Lajpat Rai wrote Urdu biographies of Mazzini, Garibaldi, Shivaji and Sri Krishna early in his career, drawing deliberate parallels between Italian unification and Indian nationalism. He spent the years of the First World War in the United States, where he founded the Indian Home Rule League of America and edited Young India, and after returning he was elected to the Central Legislative Assembly in 1926. Aurobindo Ghosh withdrew to Pondicherry in 1910 and never sat in the Assembly, Bipin Chandra Pal's foreign sojourn was in England, and Motilal Nehru wrote no such biographies.

items.value: Neither — Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship or domicile, and a number can be deactivated or omitted
items.reasoning: Aadhaar establishes only identity and residence-based enrolment; the Aadhaar Act and every Aadhaar letter state expressly that it is not proof of citizenship or of domicile, and a foreigner resident in India for the qualifying period can obtain one. Statement 2 is also wrong: the Aadhaar (Enrolment and Update) Regulations, 2016 empower the UIDAI to omit or deactivate an Aadhaar number, for instance on discovery of duplicate or defective enrolment or failure of biometric updates for children.

items.value: The Aral Sea only
items.reasoning: The Aral Sea is the standard example of a water body destroyed by human activity — Soviet-era diversion of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya for cotton irrigation shrank it to a small fraction of its 1960 extent and split it into remnant basins. The Black Sea is a large marine basin connected to the Mediterranean through the Bosporus and has not shrunk, and Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake, holds about a fifth of the planet's unfrozen surface freshwater and has suffered pollution and ecological stress but no comparable loss of water.

items.value: The World Justice Project
items.reasoning: The Rule of Law Index is the annual publication of the World Justice Project, an independent organisation that scores countries on constraints on government power, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, and civil and criminal justice. Amnesty International publishes human-rights reports rather than an index of this kind, the International Court of Justice is a judicial organ that settles inter-state disputes, and the OHCHR does not produce this index.

items.value: The National Payments Corporation of India
items.reasoning: The National Financial Switch, the network that interconnects the country's ATMs and allows a card of one bank to be used at another bank's machine, is owned and operated by the National Payments Corporation of India, which took it over from IDRBT in 2009. The Indian Banks' Association is an industry body without such an operating role, NSDL is a securities depository, and the RBI is the regulator that authorises the switch rather than the entity that runs the interconnection.

items.value: Statement 1 only — the description of CAR is right, but the ratio is prescribed by the regulator, not by each bank
items.reasoning: Statement 1 correctly describes the capital adequacy ratio as the cushion of a bank's own capital, measured against its risk-weighted assets, that absorbs losses when borrowers default. Statement 2 is wrong: the minimum CAR is prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India in line with the Basel framework and is binding on every bank; an individual bank may hold more than the minimum but cannot decide the requirement for itself.

items.value: Both — open APIs make the platform device-agnostic, and iris is one of the supported online authentication modes
items.reasoning: Aadhaar authentication is exposed as a public, open API over the internet, so any application on any connected device — a point-of-sale terminal, a micro-ATM, a mobile handset or a desktop — can be built to call it, which is the sense in which statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is straightforwardly correct: UIDAI supports demographic, OTP and biometric authentication, and the biometric modes include both fingerprint and iris. The judgement call is the sweeping phrase 'any electronic device' in statement 1; read strictly it is an overstatement, and on that stricter reading the answer would be B.

items.value: Yemen and South Sudan
items.reasoning: Both countries were the focus of the 2017 famine emergency: famine was formally declared in parts of South Sudan amid its civil war and ethnic violence, and Yemen's war left millions facing acute malnutrition and the world's largest food-security crisis alongside a cholera epidemic. Angola and Zambia, Morocco and Tunisia were not in conflict-driven famine; Venezuela's severe food shortages arose from economic collapse rather than war or ethnic conflict, and Colombia was not affected in this way.

items.value: Statements 1 and 2 only — grants-in-aid and universities were recommended, but English was not prescribed at all levels
items.reasoning: Wood's Despatch of 1854 introduced the grants-in-aid system to bring privately managed schools within a state-supervised framework, and recommended universities on the London model, which led to the founding of the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras universities in 1857. Statement 3 misstates its language policy: the Despatch prescribed the vernaculars as the medium at the primary and lower levels and English at the higher levels, and is remembered precisely for endorsing vernacular instruction at the base of the system rather than English throughout.

items.value: The Committee on Subordinate Legislation
items.reasoning: Scrutiny of delegated or subordinate legislation — rules, regulations, sub-rules and by-laws framed by the executive under powers conferred by the Constitution or by a statute — is precisely the mandate of the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, which reports to the House whether those powers are being exercised within the limits of the delegation. The Committee on Government Assurances follows up promises made by ministers on the floor, the Rules Committee deals with the House's own rules of procedure, and the Business Advisory Committee allocates time for government business.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the TET requirement is right, but qualifications are laid down by the central academic authority and most teacher-education institutions are private
items.reasoning: Section 23(1) of the Right to Education Act vests the power to lay down minimum teacher qualifications in an academic authority authorised by the Central Government, and that authority is the National Council for Teacher Education, not any State Council, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 is correct: the NCTE notification issued under that section makes passing the Teacher Eligibility Test a mandatory qualification for appointment as a primary teacher. Statement 3 inverts the reality documented by the Justice Verma Commission — the overwhelming majority of teacher-education institutions in India are privately managed self-financing bodies, not institutions run directly by State Governments.

items.value: Pairs 1 and 2 — Chapchar Kut is Mizo and Khongjom Parba is Manipuri; Thang-Ta is Manipur's, not Sikkim's
items.reasoning: Chapchar Kut is the spring festival of the Mizos, celebrated in Mizoram after the clearing of jhum fields, so pair 1 is right. Khongjom Parba is the Manipuri ballad tradition, sung to the dholak, that narrates the Anglo-Manipuri battle of Khongjom in 1891, so pair 2 is right. Pair 3 is wrong: Thang-Ta, the sword-and-spear martial art performed as dance, belongs to Manipur, not Sikkim.

items.value: Statement 1 only — the 2006 Act did replace the 1954 Act, but the FSSAI is not headed by the Director General of Health Services
items.reasoning: The Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 consolidated a set of earlier food laws, the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 among them, and repealed them, so statement 1 is correct. Statement 2 is wrong on the FSSAI's structure: the Authority is administered by a Chairperson and a Chief Executive Officer and works under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, but it is a separate statutory body and is not placed under the charge of the Director General of Health Services.

items.value: Israel
items.reasoning: The 'two-state solution' is the long-standing formula for the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, under which an independent State of Palestine would exist alongside the State of Israel, broadly along the pre-1967 lines. It is not the vocabulary used for China, whose Taiwan question is framed as 'one China', nor for Iraq or Yemen, whose conflicts are discussed in terms of federalism or power-sharing rather than the creation of two states.

items.value: Statement 2 only — the eldest woman aged 18 or above heads the household for the ration card; the BPL-only and 1600-calorie claims are wrong
items.reasoning: Section 13(1) of the National Food Security Act, 2013 makes the eldest woman of the household, being not less than eighteen years of age, the head of household for the purpose of issuing ration cards, so statement 2 is correct. Statement 1 is wrong because the Act covers up to 75 per cent of the rural and 50 per cent of the urban population through priority households and Antyodaya families, a far wider net than BPL alone. Statement 3 misquotes Schedule II, which entitles pregnant women and lactating mothers to a take-home ration of about 600 calories, not 1600.
